question: A 22-year-old student has difficulty reading the blackboard but sees near objects clearly. Retinoscopy confirms myopia. Which type of corrective lens is prescribed and why?

answers.text: Convex (plus) lens, to increase convergence of light rays onto the retina

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A convex lens would move the focus further back, worsening myopia. Plus lenses are used for hypermetropia and presbyopia.

answers.text: Concave (minus) lens, to diverge light rays so that the focal point falls on the retina rather than in front of it

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In myopia the eye has excess refracting power — light focuses in front of the retina. A concave lens diverges incoming light, effectively moving the focal point back onto the retina.

answers.text: Cylindrical lens, to correct the unequal meridional refracting power

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cylindrical lenses correct astigmatism. Simple myopia is corrected with spherical concave lenses.

answers.text: Prism, to redirect the visual axis toward the fixation target

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Prisms correct deviation of the visual axis (e.g., in strabismus), not refractive errors.

overallFeedback.feedback: Myopia means the eye's focal point falls in front of the retina. A concave (minus/diverging) lens corrects this by reducing the effective refracting power.
Well done. Myopia = excessive power → concave (minus) lens to reduce convergence. Hypermetropia = insufficient power → convex (plus) lens to increase convergence.
